name: websocket/sessions
about: What a server does on its WebSocket transport, where one socket carries many batches and outlives each of them. A client routes frames by op id and learns a schema change from a close, so an answer without an id, a cancel that ends more than it names, or an RB dictionary nobody checked leaves a client waiting for ever or reading every answer under the wrong names, with nothing failing.
source: spec 04 §5 (the transport, cancel, a batch refused as a whole, capability expiry, the schema parameter and 4409), spec 12 §3.1 (1007), spec 05 §3 (the status a refusing viewer hook's code derives) and spec 06 §6 (caps.exp). Written from those sections, not from either runtime.
rule: The socket is opened at /rayfold/ws with subprotocol rayfold.0.1. The viewer hook answers each case's `viewer`, or refuses as `hook` says, before the upgrade.

`connect.schema` is sent as the `schema` query parameter of the socket URL: `$server` stands for the server's schema hash, `$public` for the hash of the schema its public manifest serves (policy expressions hidden), anything else is sent as written. A hash other than those two is closed with 4409 and the server's hash as the reason.

Steps run in order. `send` writes a text message holding that JSON; `sendHex` writes a text message holding exactly those bytes; `command` runs that operation against the same server from another client, as a change a live query must hear; `clock` sets the server's clock (epoch milliseconds); `expect` reads the next frames, which must be these, compared per op id in order; `close` reads the server's close frame; `ran` checks how many times each resolver ran.

In an expected frame, the top-level members must be exactly those of the frame the server sent; `error` is compared by its `code` (the message is free text), and the value "*" accepts anything present.

Resolvers: `book` and `pricey` answer the row of `data` with that id, or null; `restock` adds `qty` to that row's stock and answers the row. The server's budget is `budget`, and its clock starts at `clock`.
schema:
entity Book { id: ID stock: Int }
query book(id: ID): Book? @allow(read: viewer != null)
query pricey(id: ID): Book? @cost(base: 50)
command restock(id: ID, qty: Int): Book

cases.name: a text message that is not UTF-8 closes the socket with 1007 and runs nothing
cases.why: a batch whose bytes are not UTF-8 read with replacement characters would run as something the client never sent. The bytes are {"ops":[{"id":1,"op":"book","args":{"id":"b?"}}]} with the ? a lone 0x80 byte

cases.name: guard: the same batch in valid UTF-8 is answered
a schema hash that is not the server's closes the socket with 4409 and the server's hash
cases.why: RB keys are numbered from the schema, and a socket has no Rayfold-Schema header: a client holding another schema would read every answer under the wrong field names. The close follows the upgrade because a browser cannot read a refused handshake

cases.name: the server's own schema hash is accepted
the public manifest's schema hash is accepted
cases.why: the manifest hides policy expressions, so its schema hashes differently, but it holds the same names and so the same RB keys. A client given only the manifest, as 0.2.1 clients are, must keep its socket

cases.name: cancel stops the op it names, and the other op of its batch keeps running
cases.why: both servers cancelled every op of the batch the named op came in, so the other live query ended with it

cases.name: a batch over budget is refused for each op id it named
cases.why: a socket carries several batches and a client routes by op id: the one refusal without an id that HTTP sends belongs to none of them, and the batch's ops would wait for a fin for ever

cases.name: a batch naming an unknown operation is refused for each op id it named
a bad envelope is refused for each op id it named
cases.why: the second op has no id, so the envelope is refused; the first op's id is still the client's to route by

cases.name: ops that carry no usable id get the refusal without one, and the socket keeps serving
cases.why: an envelope whose ops are not objects ended a Node server, thrown out of the socket's data handler

cases.name: a viewer hook that refuses as unauthenticated answers the handshake 401
cases.why: a refused token is answered as HTTP answers it: the status the code derives, before the socket opens

cases.name: a viewer hook that fails otherwise answers the handshake 500
a capability's socket ends at its exp: open ops end unauthenticated, a later batch is refused per op, and the socket closes with 1008
cases.why: the token was valid when the socket opened, and a socket that outlived it would serve its live queries for good

cases.name: guard: before its exp a capability's socket is served
